subtitle: Sometimes one thing causes the other. Often it doesn't.

steps.label: SAYS NOTHING ABOUT WHICH DRIVES WHICH
SPEARMAN FOR CURVED / OUTLIER-PRONE DATA
steps.sub: Works on ranks instead of raw values

eyebrow: Ad spend vs. sales, colored by the hidden confounder
caption: Real output: the strong-looking trend is really season driving BOTH variables at once.

eyebrow: A correlation with NO causal link
code:
ads = 1000 + 3000*season + noise     # season drives spend
sales = 20000 + 30000*season + noise  # season drives sales too
r, p = stats.pearsonr(ads, sales)
print(round(r, 3))   # 0.819 -- looks like ads strongly predict sales
caption: Ads have ZERO real effect on sales in this simulation -- season confounds both.
Correlate what's left after removing season's effect -- collapses to essentially zero.

code:
u = rng.uniform(0, 1, 365)
ads_r = 1000 + 3000 * u   # spend assigned by LOTTERY, not season
print(round(np.corrcoef(ads_r, sales)[0,1], 3))   # 0.026
caption: Random assignment cancels EVERY confounder, measured or not -- why A/B tests are the gold standard.

eyebrow: Correlation can also MISS real relationships
code:
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 200)
y = x ** 2 + noise   # y is almost ENTIRELY determined by x
print(round(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0,1], 3))   # -0.165 -- looks weak!
caption: r only sees straight lines. A perfect U-shape can look like nothing. Always plot the data.
